summary: Lime Rock Light at the mouth of Newport Harbor (1854-1927), kept for 32-34 years by Ida Lewis, the Grace Darling of America. Now the Ida Lewis Yacht Club.

structures.note: Thirteen feet (4.0 m) high and four feet square, attached to the keeper's dwelling. The NRHP nomination dates the present tower and dwelling to 1857.

access.note: Private yacht club. The NRHP form lists accessibility as 'yes, restricted'; the USLHS record says it is not open to the public.

events.note: Hosea Lewis became keeper on 8 December 1853 (1869 Tribune).
Brick tower. The USLHS record gives 1854; the NRHP dates the present tower to 1857.
Two soldiers from Fort Adams rescued on 20 March 1869 by Ida Lewis and her brother Hosey. The boy who had taken them out in a sailboat drowned.
A sheep and three men went into trouble from a wharf in a gale; Ida Lewis rescued them (National Archives account). The Tribune dates what appears to be the same rescue to January 1867.
Two soldiers who had broken through the ice near Lime Rock rescued on 4 February 1881 (Life-Saving Service award list).
Mrs. R. P. Walker of Long Island rescued at a Newport wharf, January 1907.
Evard Jansen keeper from 1911 (USLHS roster; Commissioner of Lighthouses 1918).
Ida Lewis Wilson died at the light in October 1911. The date is disputed: 14 October (NRHP), 24 October (National Archives account).
Lime Rock renamed Ida Lewis Rock by the Rhode Island legislature (National Archives account; the NRHP says renamed after her death).
The light and lens were removed from the tower (NRHP).
Replaced by an automatic beacon on a steel skeletal tower directly in front of the lighthouse (NRHP).
Sold to the Narragansett Bay Regatta Association, which set up the Ida Lewis Yacht Club (NRHP).
The lamp Ida Lewis used was found at the Staten Island depot and returned to Newport as a loan to the yacht club.
Coast Guard automatic beacon discontinued and taken down on 1 November 1963 (NRHP).
Full restoration of the cupola housing the light, completed spring 2023 (Lime Rock Foundation).

keepers.name: Hosea Lewis
keepers.note: A veteran ex-revenue pilot (1869 Tribune). The Tribune gives 8 December 1853 as his start; the NRHP has him moving his family to the rock in 1858 and paralysed by a stroke six months later. The Tribune dates the stroke four months after June 1857.

keepers.name: Zoradia Lewis
keepers.note: Archive prints 'Zoradia Lewis'. The National Archives account calls Hosea's wife 'Zorada' and says she and Ida carried out the lighthouse duties. The archive does not state the relationship, so the story does not assert it.

keepers.name: Idawalley Zoradia Lewis
keepers.note: Known as Ida Lewis. Married William Wilson of Black Rock, Conn., on 23 October 1870 (Providence Morning Star notice); separated after about two years (National Archives account). Newspapers after 1900 call her Ida Lewis Wilson. Died 1911 at the light; the day is disputed.

keepers.name: T. Rudolph Lewis
keepers.note: Roster line only. The 1869 Tribune names a brother Rudolph; no source read ties this line to him.

keepers.name: Evard Jansen
keepers.note: Printed as 'E. Jansen, keeper, Lime Rock Light Station, R. I.' in the Commissioner of Lighthouses report for fiscal 1918.

wrecks.outcome: Two soldiers from Fort Adams, Sergeant James Adams and Private John McLaughlin, rescued by Ida Lewis and her brother Hosey after their boat overturned in a gale. The 14-year-old boy who had taken them out drowned.
Two soldiers who had broken through the ice near Lime Rock rescued; the Life-Saving Service award list credits her.

Ida Lewis rescued all four in a boat that got into trouble after a sheep went into the water from the wharf, per the National Archives account. The Tribune describes what appears to be the same rescue in January 1867.
Mrs. R. P. Walker of Long Island rescued after she slipped between a boat and the wharf at Newport.

corrections.proposed: Remove. The light was first lit in 1854; 1927 is the date the light and lens were removed and an automatic beacon took over.
corrections.why: The NRHP and the USLHS record both give 1854 for the first light.
The NRHP describes a 300-foot wooden pier from the mainland to the rock, with boat slips on the east side.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata's first-lit year of 1927 is the date of the automatic beacon that replaced the 1854 light. The 1854 date is supported by the NRHP and the USLHS record.

1927: the light and lens were removed and the automatic beacon took over (NRHP; USLHS). 1963: the Coast Guard's automatic beacon was discontinued and taken down. Both dates are sourced for different things.
The USLHS record gives the brick tower 1854. The NRHP says 'the present tower and dwelling date from 1857.' The record keeps 1854 and the NRHP date is noted.

The 1869 Tribune gives 8 December 1853 as the day he became keeper; the NRHP has the family moving to the rock on 29 July 1858. The roster begins in 1853. These are different events (appointment and family residence).

The Tribune: four months after the family joined in June 1857. The NRHP: six months after the family moved in July 1858. The National Archives account: a few months after the appointment. The sources disagree; the story says so.
14 October 1911 (NRHP) against 24 October 1911 (National Archives). A Pascoag paper of 27 October says the death came 'this week', which supports the later date.
The Bulletin of 1925 gives 32 years; the NRHP gives 34; 1879-1911 by the roster is 32. The story gives the range.
The 1869 Tribune: a stormy afternoon, with her brother Hosey at the oars. The 1911 feature: a stormy morning, with Ida alone launching her dory. The story gives both.
The National Archives account: the Rhode Island legislature renamed the rock in 1924. The NRHP: the light was renamed after her death in 1911. Both are given.
The NRHP: approximately 100 yards offshore. The 1869 Tribune: about 304 yards from the shore. Both are given.
The NRHP gives 1927 for the removal of the light and lens and 1928 for the light being discontinued. The story says the year is not settled.

The National Archives account dates the wharf and sheep rescue to 1877. The Tribune describes what appears to be the same rescue in January 1867. The story states the disagreement and does not pick a year.
The Lime Rock Foundation dates the lighthouse to 1853; the USLHS record and the NRHP give 1854. The story states both.
The National Archives account gives 1924 (legislature); the NRHP says the light was renamed after her death in 1911. The story states both and does not reconcile them.

notes_for_editor: 1. Medal table: the 1895 Life-Saving Service award table (scan p. 256 of lifesavingservic06unitrich) is an OCR'd multi-column table. The row for Ida Lewis (name and station: 'Ida Lewis-Wilson', 'Keeper of Lime Rock light-house, Newport, R.I.') is legible, but the medal kind and date (a 'July 16,1881' date in the same block) cannot be matched to her row from the text, and the page image was not viewed. The story no longer gives a medal date from the table; it uses only the rescue credit (line quoted in the story) and the National Archives account of her medals. A reviewer who has the page image can add the medal date if it checks out. 2. Lighthouse Board 1901: the volume has no archive.org page index. The Light-House exhibit list is on printed page 42 (verified from the OCR's page markers). The scan page 54 in the earlier draft could not be confirmed and was dropped. 3. Sheep rescue: the Tribune (12 April 1869 article, 'The next rescue was ... January, 1867') and the National Archives blog (1877) describe what look like the same rescue. The story states the disagreement. 4. First rescue: the 1869 Tribune gives an 1839 rescue at 'when she was only 17', which conflicts with the 1842 birth date in the same article. Not used. 5. Zoradia Lewis (roster 1872-1879): the archive's name. The National Archives account calls Hosea's wife 'Zorada' and says she and Ida ran the light. The archive does not say she is Hosea's wife, so the story does not say so. 6. T. Rudolph Lewis (roster 1911): roster line only. The 1869 Tribune names a brother Rudolph; no source read connects the two. 7. The 1911 Olneyville feature is a syndicated article with errors (for example, it says she was 'for 60 years keeper'). Used only to show that later accounts differ. 8. The USCG Historian's biography returned only the Wayback frame, so it was not read. 9. Lighthouse Board annual reports before 1891 are not in the local corpus; 1853-1879 facts rest on the 1869 Tribune, the roster, the National Archives account and the USLHS record. 10. Wikipedia (lead only) says the original Fresnel lens is at the Museum of Newport History; not verified and not used. 11. The Lime Rock Foundation's 1853 authorization date is a secondary claim; it is stated next to the 1854 date. 12. The NRHP calls the Carnegie payment a pension by Andrew Carnegie; the 1907 News-Democrat reports a Carnegie hero fund payment and a life of $30 a month. Both are cited. 13. The Harper's Weekly issue of 31 July 1869 is cited through the NRHP; not read directly. 14. The Morning Star marriage notice's OCR reads the husband's name as 'WiliUm 11. Wilson'; the story gives only 'a Mr. Wilson'. The date '23d instant' is read as 23 October from the paper's month; that is an inference, marked as one in the text. 15. Today: the NRHP nomination is the only source for the lamp, the pier and the closed status; the story attributes them to it. 16. Living people: none named (the club's staff are not named). Mrs. R. P. Walker, a 1907 rescue case, is named as the newspaper printed her name; Mrs. Dawley is not named.
